episode_thesis: Richard Brennan argues that backtests overfit through hindsight selection and fitting to a known sequence of events and so cannot predict returns, and that only a walk-forward test on untouched out-of-sample data gives realistic drawdown (35-40% rather than 5-10%), CAGR and volatility benchmarks. He also argues that trends and mean reversion arise from collective trader impact (divergent versus convergent feedback forces) rather than from human behavioural bias, so AI agents will not end them, and that for 'outlier hunter' ensemble trend programs trade-return correlations, not price correlations, decide whether correlated markets diversify. Niels Kaastrup-Larsen adds that vol-scaled trend followers keep resizing after a volatility spike (so sell-side forced-selling estimates mislead), that convergence and systematic-macro strategies are what break in turbulence while sensible rule-based trend does not, and that the early-August 2024 shock was short and quickly reversed.

speakers.name: Richard Brennan
speakers.role: Guest co-host; Australia-based systematic trend-following manager and researcher; self-described 'outlier hunter' using ensembles of trend models

worldview_premises.premise: Backtests always overfit; they should be used for sensitivity tests across simulated regimes but never to predict future expected returns.
worldview_premises.support: Comparison of backtest versus walk-forward results in his current research phase; argument from hindsight.

worldview_premises.premise: Choosing the best of several parameter streams after the fact is a hindsight selection bias that cannot occur in live trading, and a backtest also overfits to noise and to a known sequence of events that the future will not repeat.
worldview_premises.support: Worked example with ten parameter settings over twenty years; 'we never have the road map'.

worldview_premises.premise: Out-of-sample data, once used for development, is tainted; touching it to select or change models contaminates the test and results are far more sensitive to overfitting than people realise.
worldview_premises.support: Experience with in-sample/out-of-sample workflow; criticism of data-mining packages.

worldview_premises.premise: A realistic out-of-sample equity curve resembles other managers' live track records, and its drawdown is much bigger (35-40%) than the backtest's (5-10%).
worldview_premises.support: His own comparison (1970-2000 in-sample, 2000-2024 out-of-sample); 'trust me it is much bigger'. No dataset or specification given.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following depends on regime: in unfavourable regimes expect stagnation and drawdowns, so a volatile equity curve is normal and a straight line should not be expected; mean reversion modellers can expect no out-of-sample decay but trend followers cannot.
worldview_premises.support: Trends arrive irregularly; contrast with mean-reversion testing practice.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend followers' weak point is psychology, not the models: overriding rules causes errors, so discipline and patience are required.
worldview_premises.support: Plane-turbulence analogy and years of discussion on the podcast.

worldview_premises.premise: Medium- to long-term trend following is more robust and has performed better than shorter-term trend following.
worldview_premises.support: 'All the data that I've seen' (not cited).

worldview_premises.premise: Trends exist in any complex adaptive system, so human behavioural bias (prospect theory) is a symptom rather than the root cause; trends and mean reversion come from trader impact, the pressure of orders that must be matched.
worldview_premises.support: First-principles, physics-style argument; fundamentals and behaviour are 'derivative reasons'.

worldview_premises.premise: Price impact is nonlinear (square-root law, Bouchaud), and groups of traders (trend followers, mean reverters, fundamental investors, HFT) exert collective forces whose combination moves price.
worldview_premises.support: Bouchaud microstructure research cited.

worldview_premises.premise: Markets are nonstationary: the mix of participant groups changes as traders enter and leave, so the balance of divergent (positive-feedback) and convergent (negative-feedback) pressure shifts.
worldview_premises.support: Reference to Andrew Lo's adaptive markets hypothesis.

worldview_premises.premise: Market structure falls into three states: divergent wins (trend), convergent wins (mean reversion), or noise when neither wins and there is no directional move.
worldview_premises.support: Conceptual framework.

worldview_premises.premise: In strong trends participants switch style to join them, amplifying the signal; so too many trend followers make trends more extreme, not extinct, while enough mean reverters can dissipate their own edge and the trend's.
worldview_premises.support: Feedback-loop reasoning; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: AI agents also exert impact, so trends and mean reversion will persist and AI will not remove them.
worldview_premises.support: Extension of the agent-based, trader-impact view.

worldview_premises.premise: Outliers are volatile and need an ensemble of models to extract; tiny differences in initial price paths (butterfly effect) produce widely dispersed trade results, so highly price-correlated markets can still have uncorrelated strategy returns.
worldview_premises.support: Brent versus WTI example with his own ensemble; nonlinear-mechanics analogy.

worldview_premises.premise: Publicly shown backtests (for example on Twitter) are beautiful equity curves; the industry should demand realism, since one never sees a bad backtest.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of social media and of a guest's remark that you never see a bad backtest.

mechanism_chains.topic: Why backtests mislead and what walk-forward testing fixes

steps.from: Full history laid out in hindsight
steps.to: Selection among parameter streams and overfitting to noise and event order
steps.why: The tester can pick the best stream and fit the known path; live trading has no such option.

steps.from: Selected, overfit backtest
steps.to: Upward-biased forward expectation and an unrealistically small drawdown

steps.from: Develop on 1970-2000 only, then run untouched on 2000-2024
steps.to: Benchmarks for drawdown, CAGR and volatility that resemble live track records
steps.why: Out-of-sample data simulates the right-hand side of the chart.

steps.from: Touching out-of-sample data to select or change models
steps.to: Contamination and overfitting return

mechanism_chains.evidence: His own comparisons of backtest, out-of-sample and adaptive curves; figures (35-40% vs 5-10% drawdown) given without dataset or rules.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Out-of-sample data is reused for selection; also for trend followers one cannot expect no out-of-sample deterioration the way mean-reversion modellers do (regime dependence).

mechanism_chains.topic: Trader impact, divergent versus convergent forces and why trends persist

steps.from: Buyers and sellers must be matched
steps.to: Price moves through order pressure, scaling with size by a square-root law

steps.from: Groups of traders with the same model
steps.to: Collective force that amplifies (divergent, positive feedback) or dissipates (convergent, negative feedback) trends

steps.from: A strong trend gets going
steps.to: Mean reverters and others switch to trend, amplifying it
steps.why: Fear of missing out; style switching.

steps.from: Enough mean reverters oppose a trend
steps.to: Trend signal dissipates and a reversion to equilibrium follows
steps.why: Convergence signals fight the prior trend.

steps.from: Neither side dominates
steps.to: Noise with no directional move

mechanism_chains.topic: Outlier hunting with ensembles: why correlated markets diversify

steps.from: Outlier (anomaly) with nonlinear, volatile price path
steps.to: A single trend model is snagged by volatility and misses the move
steps.why: Needs many models to maximise extraction.

steps.from: Tiny differences in initial price paths
steps.to: Widely dispersed trade results in nonlinear territory
steps.why: Butterfly effect; trade correlation, not price correlation, matters.

steps.from: Same ensemble on Brent and WTI
steps.to: Quite uncorrelated return streams despite highly correlated prices

steps.from: Strong outlier trend
steps.to: Hold and pyramid with more models, accept big give-back at the turn

mechanism_chains.evidence: His own test of an ensemble on Brent and crude (no numbers) and the 2024 cocoa episode.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Not stated; he says the conventional wisdom is right for nearly all other models.

decision_process.practice: Develop and test models on in-sample data only (e.g. 1970-2000, multi-market over 30 years and about 100 markets); run the frozen models once on out-of-sample data (2000-2024) and never touch it afterwards.
decision_process.why: In-sample needs a lot of data for robustness; out-of-sample is the crucible for the whole process.

decision_process.practice: Compare three curves: the backtest ('pink unicorn'), the out-of-sample curve, and an adaptive workflow that periodically re-estimates in-sample and walks forward; set drawdown, CAGR and volatility expectations from the out-of-sample curve.
decision_process.why: Realistic benchmark; the backtest is always best and unrealistic.

decision_process.practice: Use backtests only for sensitivity tests across simulated regimes, not for expected-return forecasts; avoid data-mining packages that overfit and then try to remove it.
Prefer medium- to long-term trend following and treat short-term trading as different from trend following.
decision_process.why: Data he has seen suggest more robust and better performance.

decision_process.practice: Run an ensemble of trend models per market for outliers; hold and pyramid with more systems getting in as the trend persists.
decision_process.why: A single system is snagged out by outlier volatility; ensemble maximises extraction.

decision_process.practice: Trade highly price-correlated markets (Brent and WTI) together when the ensemble's trade returns are uncorrelated.
decision_process.why: Trade correlation, not price correlation, determines diversification for outlier hunters.

decision_process.practice: Does not resize positions down with rising volatility after entry (cocoa 2024: held and added); accepts the big give-back when the trend turns.
decision_process.why: Outlier hunters stay with the trend; selling would miss the extreme move.

decision_process.practice: Follow the rules, with discipline and patience; do not override models under stress.

speakers.evidence_style: Argument from first principles and analogy (hindsight, physics of price impact, butterfly effect), and his own in-house walk-forward and ensemble tests reported without data; cites academic ideas (Bouchaud, Lo) and anecdotes such as cocoa.

current_views.view: The early-August 2024 volatility shock was a short, sharp event that reversed quickly; trend models adapt fast and would have been well placed in a prolonged downtrend.
current_views.reasoning: Trend followers were hit by the yen, Nikkei and Nasdaq early on but trends resumed.

current_views.view: The August losses came from the Nikkei, yen and equity indexes; equity indexes recovered within the month while the yen and Nikkei stayed down, and commodities kept trending well.
Monthly statistics hide intra-month volatility, so a month with a violent shock can look benign in the records.
AI will not end trends or mean reversion; they are here to stay.
current_views.reasoning: AI agents are traders whose orders exert impact.

speakers.role: Host of Top Traders Unplugged; veteran hedge fund manager; creator of the Trend Barometer

worldview_premises.premise: Vol-scaled trend followers become more defensive after a quick volatile event and keep selling after volatility rises even if prices recover, so a bounce does not mean a symmetric re-buy.
worldview_premises.support: How volatility-targeted sizing works; 'some of us' resize, 'you don't'.

worldview_premises.premise: Sell-side estimates of forced CTA equity selling (about $170B) are misleading because they ignore ongoing volatility-driven sizing and do not imply CTAs simply buy everything back.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoning from vol-targeted sizing; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: No market event breaks a rule-based trend system with sensible, tested (not AI-optimised) rules; drawdowns are painful but do not break the models, while convergence strategies and systematic macro tend to break in turbulence.
worldview_premises.support: Decades of trend history; the airplane-turbulence analogy (damage is inside, not structural).

worldview_premises.premise: Investor pressure for smoother returns pushes trend programs to add non-trend models such as carry, which dilutes the pure trend profile and may explain dispersion between managers.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of the industry; he expects August dispersion to show it.

worldview_premises.premise: Volatility dampening and research that lowers drawdown are acceptable only if they do not change the long-term return profile or cause style drift; otherwise they just lower expectations.
worldview_premises.support: Aircraft-stabiliser analogy (stay on course).

worldview_premises.premise: True diversification into commodities matters: managers concentrated in financials (to hold large AUM) suffered more in August.
worldview_premises.support: Cross-manager observation in the month.

worldview_premises.premise: Endogenous flows explain big moves more than exogenous news (Bouchaud), which fits the 2024 cocoa run in which global macro funds bought while dynamic-sizing trend followers sold.
worldview_premises.support: Bouchaud's conclusion as the host recalls it; cocoa episode.

worldview_premises.premise: Social-media backtests are unlikely to reproduce; big managers use some walk-forward process.
worldview_premises.support: Industry knowledge; not documented.

worldview_premises.premise: Not all managers use VaR-style volatility-sensitive risk models, so the market is not forced into synchronised selling.
worldview_premises.support: 'A lot of people do but not everyone.'

decision_process.practice: Vol-scaled trend sizing: resize continuously with volatility rather than hold size fixed after entry.

decision_process.practice: Accept risk-reducing research (vol adjustment, lower drawdown) only if it leaves the long-term return profile and style unchanged.

The calm may be the quiet before the storm when it really gets hairy; the quick volatile event is lucky because it leaves trend followers more defensive.

disagreements.topic: Why trends exist: behavioural bias versus trader impact

positions.speaker: Richard Brennan
positions.position: Behavioural bias (prospect theory) and fundamentals are symptoms; the root cause is trader impact and collective order flow, which AI agents will also exert.

positions.speaker: Conventional view as characterised by Brennan
positions.position: Trends come from behavioural bias (fear and greed) and from fundamental drivers; AI might make markets efficient enough to end trends.

disagreements.topic: Whether highly price-correlated markets add diversification

positions.speaker: Richard Brennan
positions.position: True for nearly all models, but not for outlier hunters using ensembles, where trade-return correlation matters and Brent versus WTI returns are quite uncorrelated.

positions.speaker: Conventional view as characterised by Brennan
positions.position: Pick one of two highly correlated markets because diversification benefits dissipate after a certain number of markets.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: The 35-40% out-of-sample versus 5-10% backtest drawdown comparison is asserted without dataset, rules, markets or sample size; the same-period live comparison with other managers is described, not shown.

Brennan says out-of-sample results are 'close to live track records of other managers', but also that out-of-sample data cannot be reused for selection; he does not say what happens to the first-use out-of-sample result once it is used to judge a program.

Brennan's rule against hindsight selection conflicts with the practice of choosing his own program's rules after years of live experience; he does not address how the 2000-2024 period stays untouched when his own knowledge of it is in his design.
The ensemble/outlier-hunter claims (Brent versus WTI, 20 models) rest on his own test with no numbers; the butterfly-effect link is an analogy, not a test.
Cocoa: Niels's 80-90% selling claim is generalised ('trend followers generally speaking'), not measured; Brennan cannot remember the month the run turned.
Corrections applied: cocoa example speaker (Niels), and the August index numbers (SG CTA +2.1% YTD, short-term traders +0.61% YTD).
Niels says convergence strategies and systematic macro 'break' in turbulence, but also that some trend programs hold carry; the breaking claim is asserted from structure, not evidence.
Brennan asserts medium- to long-term trend following has performed better than shorter-term, but cites no data and says short-term trading is not trend following.

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) The speakers claim no forward-looking input for prices: Brennan's thesis is that backtests cannot predict the future, so expectations should come from out-of-sample drawdown, CAGR and volatility benchmarks, with regime (favourable or unfavourable for trend) as the driver. Niels reads the Trend Barometer (short timeframe), index dispersion and model speed as state indicators, and expects volatility to stay higher after a spike, keeping vol-scaled trend followers defensive. The trader-impact framework implies watching the mix of divergent and convergent participants, but no observable proxy is named.
reader_inferences: (reader) Brennan's framework suggests a test: trend returns should be higher when order-flow concentration (many participants flipping to trend) is high; no measurable proxy is proposed in the episode.

(reader) The disagreement over resizing volatility (Niels resizes, Brennan holds and pyramids) implies a testable difference in outlier-period performance: constant-risk sizing should lag in extreme trends and lose less at reversals.
(reader) Walk-forward testing as described is a single split; it is sensitive to the choice of split date (2000), which the speaker does not discuss.
